cmo-cmo-2009-01.prompt:
Given an $m \times n$ grid with squares coloured either black or white, we say that a black square in the grid is *stranded* if there is some square to its left in the same row that is white and there is some square above it in the same column that is white (see Figure 1).

*Figure 1. A $4 \times 5$ grid with no stranded black squares*

Find a closed formula for the number of $2 \times n$ grids with no stranded black squares.

cmo-cmo-2009-02.prompt: Two circles of different radii are cut out of cardboard. Each circle is subdivided into $200$ equal sectors. On each circle $100$ sectors are painted white and the other $100$ are painted black. The smaller circle is then placed on top of the larger circle, so that their centers coincide. Show that one can rotate the small circle so that the sectors on the two circles line up and at least $100$ sectors on the small circle lie over sectors of the same color on the big circle.
cmo-cmo-2009-02.answer: Over all $200$ aligned positions, each small sector lies once over each big sector, so the total number of colour matches is $100\cdot100 + 100\cdot100 = 20000$; the average is $100$, so some position has at least $100$ matches.

cmo-cmo-2009-03.prompt:
Define
$$f(x, y, z) = \frac{(xy + yz + zx)(x + y + z)}{(x + y)(x + z)(y + z)}.$$
Determine the set of real numbers $r$ for which there exists a triplet $(x, y, z)$ of positive real numbers satisfying $f(x, y, z) = r$.

cmo-cmo-2009-04.prompt: Find all ordered pairs $(a, b)$ such that $a$ and $b$ are integers and $3^a + 7^b$ is a perfect square.

cmo-cmo-2009-05.prompt: A set of points is marked on the plane, with the property that any three marked points can be covered with a disk of radius $1$. Prove that the set of all marked points can be covered with a disk of radius $1$.
cmo-cmo-2009-05.answer: A unit disk centred at $c$ covers $p$ iff $c$ lies in the unit disk $D(p)$ centred at $p$; the hypothesis says any three disks $D(p)$ intersect, so by Helly's theorem (and compactness for infinitely many points) all of them have a common point, which is the required centre.
